title: The Multiplicity Factor Theorem: (X − a)ᵏ ∣ p via Vanishing Derivatives
description: The parent (factor-remainder-theorem) proves the Factor Theorem (X − a) ∣ p ↔ p(a) = 0. Its OQ-01 asks for the multiplicity version: (X − a)ᵏ ∣ p iff p(a) = p′(a) = ⋯ = p^{(k−1)}(a) = 0, connecting the Factor Theorem to Taylor expansion via polynomial derivatives. Over a characteristic-zero field, Mathlib proves this through rootMultiplicity (le_rootMultiplicity_iff and lt_rootMultiplicity_iff_isRoot_iterate_derivative). This entry combines them into the multiplicity factor theorem, with the k = 1 (Factor Theorem) and k = 2 (double root) cases. 0 axioms.

overview.historicalContext:
The Factor Theorem states that a is a root of a polynomial p iff (X − a) divides p. Its refinement to higher multiplicity says that (X − a)ᵏ divides p iff a is a root of multiplicity at least k, which — over a field of characteristic zero — is equivalent to the vanishing of p together with its first k − 1 derivatives at a: p(a) = p′(a) = ⋯ = p^{(k−1)}(a) = 0. This is precisely the statement that the Taylor expansion of p at a begins at order k, tying the algebraic notion of multiplicity to the analytic/Taylor picture. The characteristic-zero hypothesis is essential: in positive characteristic p, the derivative of Xᵖ is zero, so derivatives can vanish without the multiplicity being large.

Mathlib formalizes root multiplicity and proves both halves of this equivalence: (X − a)ᵏ ∣ p iff k ≤ rootMultiplicity a p (le_rootMultiplicity_iff), and n < rootMultiplicity a p iff the iterated derivatives up to order n vanish at a (lt_rootMultiplicity_iff_isRoot_iterate_derivative, requiring factorials to be nonzerodivisors). This entry answers the parent's OQ-01 by combining these into the multiplicity factor theorem, with the k = 1 and k = 2 cases.
overview.problemStatement: Prove the multiplicity version of the Factor Theorem: over a characteristic-zero field, for a nonzero polynomial p and k ≥ 1, (X − a)ᵏ ∣ p iff p and its first k − 1 derivatives all vanish at a (∀ m < k, p^{(m)}(a) = 0). Record the k = 1 (Factor Theorem) and k = 2 (double root) cases.
overview.proofStrategy: Write k = n + 1. Then (X − a)^{n+1} ∣ p ↔ n + 1 ≤ rootMultiplicity a p (le_rootMultiplicity_iff) ↔ n < rootMultiplicity a p (Nat.add_one_le_iff) ↔ ∀ m ≤ n, (derivative^[m] p).IsRoot a (lt_rootMultiplicity_iff_isRoot_iterate_derivative, with (n!:K) a nonzerodivisor since K has characteristic zero). Rewriting IsRoot as eval = 0 and m ≤ n as m < n + 1 (Nat.lt_succ_iff) finishes. The k = 1 case is Mathlib's dvd_iff_isRoot; the k = 2 case instantiates the main theorem at k = 2 and unfolds the two derivatives.
keyInsights: Multiplicity = order of vanishing of the Taylor expansion: (X − a)ᵏ ∣ p iff p^{(0)}(a) = ⋯ = p^{(k−1)}(a) = 0, the analytic reading of the algebraic multiplicity.
Characteristic zero is essential — it makes every factorial a nonzerodivisor, which the derivative characterization needs; in characteristic p the derivative of Xᵖ vanishes, breaking the equivalence.
The proof factors cleanly through rootMultiplicity: divisibility ↔ a multiplicity bound (le_rootMultiplicity_iff), and that bound ↔ vanishing derivatives (the iterate-derivative iff).
The double-root criterion (X − a)² ∣ p ↔ p(a) = p′(a) = 0 is the workhorse special case, used to detect repeated roots and discriminant vanishing.
This connects the Factor Theorem to Taylor expansion exactly as the OQ requested, using Mathlib's polynomial-derivative API.

conclusion.summary: A fully verified (0 sorries, 0 axioms, no native_decide) file of 71 lines and 4 theorems proving the multiplicity factor theorem: over a characteristic-zero field, (X − a)ᵏ ∣ p iff p and its first k − 1 derivatives vanish at a. It chains Mathlib's le_rootMultiplicity_iff and the iterate-derivative characterization of multiplicity, and records the k = 1 (Factor Theorem) and k = 2 (double root) cases.
conclusion.implications: This answers the parent's OQ-01, connecting the Factor Theorem to Taylor expansion exactly as requested: multiplicity is the order of vanishing of the polynomial's derivatives. The double-root criterion is a reusable tool for detecting repeated roots (e.g. when the discriminant vanishes, or a polynomial shares a root with its derivative). The characteristic-zero hypothesis is made explicit, clarifying where the derivative characterization holds.
openQuestions: Formalize the explicit Taylor-coefficient form: the order-k Taylor coefficient of p at a is p^{(k)}(a)/k!, so (X − a)ᵏ ∣ p iff the first k Taylor coefficients vanish, via Polynomial.taylor.
Extend to positive characteristic using Hasse derivatives, where the divided-power derivatives correctly characterize multiplicity even when ordinary derivatives fail.
